The reason for this comes down to a fundamental difference in what your computer is actually doing in these two scenarios. It is the difference between **real-time rendering** (video games) and **video playback** (movies and shows). 

Here is a breakdown of why games are so demanding and movies are so easy for your graphics card (GPU) to handle:

### 1. Video Games: Real-Time Rendering
When you play a video game, your GPU is creating every single image you see from scratch, in real-time. 

Because a game is interactive, the computer doesn't know what you are going to do next. If you decide to turn your character around, throw a grenade, or look up at the sky, the GPU has to instantly calculate:
*   The 3D geometry of the objects in your view.
*   The textures and colors of those objects.
*   How the light sources bounce off different surfaces.
*   Shadows, reflections, and particle effects (like smoke or fire).

To make the game look smooth, your GPU has to do all of this math **30 to 60 times every single second** (known as 30 or 60 FPS). At 60 FPS, your graphics card has just **16 milliseconds** to build an entire, complex frame from scratch. This is an incredibly stressful and heavy workload, which is why graphics cards struggle and get hot. 

### 2. Animated Movies: Pre-Rendering and Video Playback
When you watch an animated movie like *Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse* or *Toy Story*, your graphics card is **not** rendering 3D models, calculating lighting, or simulating physics. It is simply decoding a video file and displaying flat, 2D images in a sequence. 

Displaying a pre-recorded video file is an incredibly easy task for any modern computer. But how did the movie get made in the first place? Through a process called **pre-rendering**.

When an animation studio makes a movie, they use massive warehouses full of thousands of incredibly powerful computers called "Render Farms." Because a movie is a set, non-interactive script, the computers don't have to render the images in 16 milliseconds. 

Instead, a render farm can spend **hours, or even days, calculating a single frame** of a movie. They can calculate exactly how millions of individual hairs blow in the wind, or how light perfectly refracts through a glass of water. Once the render farm finishes calculating that perfect image, it takes a "picture" of it and saves it as a flat 2D frame. Those frames are stitched together into a video file, which is sent to your TV or PC.

### The Analogy
Think of it like a math test:
*   **Playing a video game** is like being forced to solve complex calculus equations on a chalkboard, live in front of an audience, and you only have one second to solve each equation. It is incredibly stressful.
*   **Watching an animated movie** is like someone handing you a piece of paper with all the answers already perfectly written down by a team of math geniuses, and all you have to do is read the paper out loud. It requires almost no effort.

You are absolutely right, that is a great catch! The computers at the animation studio *are* doing the rendering. 

However, there are two big distinctions to make here: **whose** hardware is doing the work, and the fact that the studio's computers are **not doing it easily at all**. 

Here is why your observation is spot-on, but also why it still looks different from a video game:

### 1. They don't do it "easily"—they struggle immensely!
When you play a video game, your graphics card has to render a frame in about **16 milliseconds**. 

When an animation studio like Pixar or Disney renders a movie, their computers are doing math that is thousands of times more complex than a video game. Because the math is so heavy, those massive, incredibly powerful computers **struggle hard**. 

They don't render a frame in 16 milliseconds; it often takes them **10 to 50 hours to render a *single frame*** of a movie. (For example, in *Monsters University*, some highly detailed frames took 29 hours to render just one image!). 

So, the graphics cards/processors at the studio *are* rendering the movie, but they aren't doing it easily. They are sweating, overheating, and working at maximum capacity for days on end. You just don't see that struggle because by the time the movie reaches your screen, the hard work was finished months ago.

### 2. CPUs vs. GPUs (Historically)
Here is a fun technical fact: for a very long time, animated movies were actually **not** rendered by graphics cards (GPUs)! They were rendered by massive rooms full of **CPUs** (Central Processing Units—the main "brain" of a computer). 

Why? Because movie rendering requires an absurd amount of computer memory (RAM) to hold all the high-resolution textures, models, and complex light-bouncing physics (Ray Tracing). Historically, GPUs didn't have enough memory to hold a whole movie scene, but CPUs could tap into massive pools of system memory. 

It is only in recent years that animation studios have started shifting toward using GPUs to render movies, because modern professional GPUs (which cost tens of thousands of dollars each) finally have enough memory and power to handle it.

### Summary
You are completely correct that computers are rendering the movie. But the reason it feels like your PC can play a movie "so easily" compared to a game is because **your** graphics card is just pressing "play" on a video file. The actual rendering was done months ago by a warehouse full of supercomputers that took hours to calculate a single second of footage!
